--- title: "Loss functions" description: "A fit makes one number as small as it can: the loss, averaged over the data. Squared and absolute error weigh the same misses very differently, so choosing between them is part of the science." order: 1 categories: [optimisation] --- ## Every fit makes one number small Each model in [Supervised learning](../03-supervised-learning/index.qmd) was fitted by an algorithm that tried values for the model's parameters until one number was as small as it could make it. That number measures how wrong the predictions are, and its formula decides which observations the model pays most attention to. This page shows the two common choices, squared and absolute error, drawing two different lines through the same data, and how to choose between them. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## From one miss to the whole dataset The **residual** is how far one prediction missed: the observed value minus the predicted one. A station with 7 animals and a prediction of 4 has a residual of 3; with a prediction of 9, a residual of −2. A **loss function** turns a residual into a penalty: zero for a perfect prediction, and larger the worse the miss. The two common ones treat large misses very differently. - **Squared error** multiplies the residual by itself. A miss of 10 costs 100, a hundred times a miss of 1. - **Absolute error** drops the sign. A miss of 10 costs 10, ten times a miss of 1. A loss scores one prediction, and a fit needs one number for the whole dataset, so the algorithm averages the loss over every observation. That average is the **objective**, and fitting means finding the parameter values that make it smallest. For squared error the objective is the mean squared error, whose square root is the RMSE that [Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) reported. ::: {.diagram} ![A residual is how far one prediction missed. A loss turns it into a penalty, and squared error grows much faster than absolute error as the miss grows. The objective averages the loss over all the data, and the fit is the parameter value that makes it smallest.](img/loss-to-fit.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Residual, the size of one miss: residual equals observed minus predicted; a line through scattered points, with a dashed segment from one point down to the line labelled residual; positive above the line, negative below it. Loss, the penalty for one miss: squared or absolute error; a steep U-shaped curve labelled squared and a shallow V labelled absolute, meeting at a residual of zero; squared error grows fast with the miss, absolute error grows in step. Objective, the average over all data: objective equals average loss; a U-shaped curve against a parameter, its lowest point marked the fit. A note says: change the loss, and the fit changes with it."} ::: An objective can also carry a penalty on the parameters themselves, which keeps them small. [MAP estimation](map-and-priors.qmd), later in this section, shows where such a penalty comes from. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With $y_i$ the observed value at station $i$, $\hat{y}_i$ the prediction and $n$ stations, the two objectives are $$\text{mean squared error} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \qquad\qquad \text{mean absolute error} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert y_i - \hat{y}_i \rvert$$ For a straight line, $\hat{y}_i = a + b\,x_i$, and fitting means choosing the intercept $a$ and slope $b$ that make the chosen objective smallest. ::: ## Worked example We fit a straight line of abundance against chlorophyll twice, changing only the loss. `optim()` is R's general-purpose search: given a function of the intercept and slope, it tries values until the function is as small as it can make it. [The next two pages](parameter-estimation.qmd) show how a search like this works. ### Two losses, two lines ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> select(abundance, chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> drop_na() # Fit a + b * chlorophyll by making the average loss smallest. fit_loss <- function(data, loss) { objective <- function(par) { residual <- data$abundance - (par[1] + par[2] * data$chlorophyll_mg_m3) mean(loss(residual)) } optim(c(0, 0), objective, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000))$par } squared <- fit_loss(d, \(r) r^2) absolute <- fit_loss(d, abs) coefs <- tibble( loss = c("Squared error", "Absolute error"), intercept = c(squared[1], absolute[1]), slope = c(squared[2], absolute[2]) ) coefs |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|loss | intercept| slope| |:--------------|---------:|-----:| |Squared error | 2.359| 1.154| |Absolute error | 1.126| 1.079|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(lm(abundance ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3, data = d)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> (Intercept) chlorophyll_mg_m3 #> 2.359 1.154 ``` ::: ::: The squared-error line starts at 2.36 animals and rises 1.15 for each mg m⁻³ of chlorophyll. The absolute-error line starts at 1.13 and rises 1.08. The squared-error line is the one `lm()` returns, and `lm()` is the engine behind `linear_reg()` in section 3: linear regression is the line that makes squared error smallest. [The next page](parameter-estimation.qmd) shows it can be found without a search. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(d, aes(chlorophyll_mg_m3, abundance)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 1.3) + geom_abline( data = coefs, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = loss), linewidth = 1 ) + labs( x = "Chlorophyll (mg m⁻³)", y = "Abundance (animals)", colour = NULL, title = "One dataset, two losses, two lines" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The two fitted lines over the 749 stations with chlorophyll measured. A few very large catches pull the squared-error line up; the absolute-error line follows the bulk of the stations, most of which caught only a few animals.](loss-functions_files/figure-html/fig-two-lines-1.png){#fig-two-lines fig-alt='A scatter plot of abundance against chlorophyll for 749 stations. Most points lie low, in a dense cloud near the origin, with a scatter of large catches up to 40 animals. Two fitted lines rise from left to right; the squared-error line sits above the absolute-error line.' width=1400} ::: ::: ### A few stations dominate squared error The two lines differ because squared error gives most of its weight to the largest misses. We can measure how much. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} residual <- d$abundance - (squared[1] + squared[2] * d$chlorophyll_mg_m3) worst <- order(abs(residual), decreasing = TRUE)[1:round(0.05 * nrow(d))] share <- c( squared = sum(residual[worst]^2) / sum(residual^2), absolute = sum(abs(residual[worst])) / sum(abs(residual)) ) round(share, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> squared absolute #> 0.497 0.210 ``` ::: ::: The 37 stations with the largest misses, 5% of the data, supply 50% of the total squared error but only 21% of the total absolute error. Half of what the squared-error fit tries to reduce comes from those few stations. ### One station moves the slope ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d_minus <- d |> slice(-which.max(abundance)) slopes <- tibble( loss = c("Squared error", "Absolute error"), `all stations` = c(squared[2], absolute[2]), `largest catch removed` = c(fit_loss(d_minus, \(r) r^2)[2], fit_loss(d_minus, abs)[2]) ) |> mutate(change = `largest catch removed` / `all stations` - 1) slopes |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|loss | all stations| largest catch removed| change| |:--------------|------------:|---------------------:|------:| |Squared error | 1.154| 0.998| -0.135| |Absolute error | 1.079| 1.057| -0.021|
::: ::: Removing the largest catch, 40 animals at one station out of 749, moves the squared-error slope from 1.15 to 1.00, a change of 13.5%. The same deletion moves the absolute-error slope by 2.1%. ## The loss is a choice about the science Neither loss is wrong. Squared error is sensitive to extreme values and absolute error is not, and the right one depends on what the large catches are. - **A real aggregation.** Fish shoal, and the big hauls may be the most important observations, for biomass or for a quota. Squared error is right, and its sensitivity is the point. - **Noise, or a net that fished badly.** Then squared error hands half of the objective to the least trustworthy stations, and absolute error is safer. A third loss, Huber, is squared for small misses and absolute for large ones, a compromise between the two. The data rarely say which case you have, so the choice comes from knowing how the survey was done. State the loss and the reason for it in the methods, next to the model. ### Counts and presence have their own losses Squared and absolute error treat the outcome as a quantity that can take any value. Counts and yes-or-no outcomes cannot, and each has its own loss. | Outcome | Usual loss | Penalises most | | --- | --- | --- | | A measurement | Squared error | Large misses | | A measurement with doubtful extremes | Absolute error | Misses in proportion to their size | | A count | Poisson deviance | A miss where few animals were expected | | Presence or absence | Log loss | A confident wrong answer | **Poisson deviance** scales the penalty with the expected count. Counting 7 animals where the model expected 2 costs about 60 times as much as counting 205 where it expected 200, though both miss by 5. Poisson regression, on [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd), is fitted by making this loss smallest. **Log loss** scores a predicted probability of presence by how much probability it gave to what happened. A prediction of 0.99 at a station that turns out empty costs about 7 times as much as a prediction of 0.5. [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) is fitted under log loss, and the threshold that turns its probability into present or absent is chosen afterwards. Accuracy cannot serve as the loss, because it changes only when a prediction crosses the threshold and so gives the search no direction to move in. These losses look like a list of special cases, but they all come from one principle, which [Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) describes. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **loss** scores one prediction from its residual; the **objective** averages it over the data, and fitting means making the objective as small as possible. - Squared error prices a miss of 10 at a hundred times a miss of 1. Here the worst 5% of stations supplied 50% of the total squared error, and removing one station moved the slope by 13.5%. - Absolute error is steadier. Use it when the extremes are doubtful, and squared error when the extremes are the science. - Counts and presence have their own losses: Poisson deviance and log loss. - The loss is a scientific choice. Report it with the model. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit both losses with `depth_m` as the input instead of chlorophyll. Do the two lines disagree more or less than they did for chlorophyll? 2. Remove the five largest catches instead of one and refit. How far does each slope move now?
